extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and policymakers concerned with nationalism, democracy, and public policy
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying normative and explanatory principles about how national organization, democracy, militarism, and colonial policy should interact; aimed at evaluating national policy choices in modern states. Useful for analysis, teaching, or policy critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active national leadership in domestic policy
rubrics_metrics.description: The nation itself, as represented by its official leaders, should actively assist in preparing an adequate national domestic policy, and in organizing the machinery for its efficient execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bismarck's scheme is cited as a model: government intervention to prepare and organize policy is preferable to laissez-faire individualism when the aim is a modern industrial nation; such leadership should take institutional responsibility for planning and execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public control of strategic infrastructure
rubrics_metrics.description: Key national infrastructure (e.g., railways) should be managed in the interest of the national economic system rather than private shareholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Prussia bought railways so they 'should be managed, not in the interest of the shareholders, but in that of the national economic system.' Implication: national economic integration can justify public ownership/management of critical services.

rubrics_metrics.name: State promotion of agricultural and technical improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Government should encourage better farming methods and an educational system that directly aids industry by producing skilled scientific experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text cites spread of better farming methods (increased yields) and education producing specialists who promote industrial efficiency — state-supported technical education and diffusion of best practices are recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organisation under skilled professional leadership subordinated to national scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: Specialized lines of activity should be organized under skilled professional leadership and subordinated to their place in a comprehensive national economy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy coherence requires that sectoral activities be integrated into an overarching national plan rather than pursued as isolated private interests; avoids fragmentation of national aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Official acceptance of economic as well as political responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Official leaders should accept economic responsibility for popular welfare in addition to political leadership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author argues this 'paternalism' has accomplished its purpose in Germany; leadership that assumes economic responsibility can enhance national welfare but must balance with political legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overbearing/domineering leadership to prevent domestic opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggressive or domineering conduct by national leaders intensifies domestic opposition and may compromise national policy success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Bismarckian tradition of bullying provoked internal and external opposition; leaders must tread warily to avoid creating a schism with working-class movements (e.g., Social Democrats).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciliation of industrial democracy without sacrificing expert leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: Statesmanship must win the support of industrial democracy (working classes) without impairing the practice of expert and responsible leadership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The test is ability to integrate democratic social forces into national organization while retaining necessary professional direction; gradual conciliation preferred to abrupt concession that undermines institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realism: national aims must match national power and resources
rubrics_metrics.description: National policy should not attempt immediate accomplishment of purposes incommensurate with national power and resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful leaders avoided overreach; overambitious aims invite failure and domestic crisis. Policies should be practicable and limited by realistic calculations of means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of efficiency in national politics
rubrics_metrics.description: National politics aim primarily at efficiency — the successful use of the force resident in the state to accomplish desired purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Efficiency requires responsible use of force and the partial distribution of political power; democrats who ignore efficiency risk impractical idealism. National organization needs structures that enable effective action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsible attachment of stricter responsibilities to use of force
rubrics_metrics.description: Further development of the national principle will involve attaching stricter responsibilities to the use of force both in internal and external policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern nations control force more responsibly than earlier polities; expectation is for stricter restraint and obligation in wielding state coercion as national institutions mature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice of war when purposive, decisive, and necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: War may be justifiable when deliberately waged for necessary, defensible purposes and when it accomplishes a decisive and desirable result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author defends some historical wars (e.g., German unification wars) as legitimate national policy instruments when they unify or secure national existence; stresses deliberation and necessity rather than wanton aggression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern wars should be decisive and teach limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflicts between efficiently organized nations tend to be fought for defensible purposes and produce decisive results that teach limits of future policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because penalties of defeat are severe and costs are high, wars will be less frequent and more consequential; each conflict clarifies practicable aims and thus reduces future causes of war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colonial expansion as legitimate tutelage and safety-valve
rubrics_metrics.description: Colonial rule by European nations can be a legitimate form of tutelage for politically disorganized societies and serve as a safety-valve for restless national energies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author argues that for a while Asiatic populations may benefit from orderly government, and colonies can provide outlets for national expansion that are less likely to provoke European wars; acknowledges moral and practical limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settle colonial disputes by arbitration/conciliation where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Disputes over colonies between European powers should generally be resolved by arbitration or conciliation rather than war, because the disputants often have more to lose than to gain by hostilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fashoda is used as example where stakes did not justify war; Russia–Japan is noted as exception because stakes involved Japan's vital interests. Colonial disputes are usually suitable for peaceful settlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggressive colonial and aggressive European policy are incompatible
rubrics_metrics.description: A nation cannot simultaneously pursue aggressive colonial expansion and aggressive European ambitions without compromising its security and coherence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Colonies scatter military resources and expose a non-maritime power to vulnerability; controlling the sea is necessary to sustain overseas possessions without undermining European strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep adequate military preparedness to preserve peace
rubrics_metrics.description: Powers sincerely desirous of peace must remain as well armed as their resources and policy demand; partial diminution of military efficiency encourages belligerents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pacific Powers must avoid unilateral weakening; maintenance of sufficient force underwrites bargaining power and deters aggression — an argument against premature or partial disarmament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disarmament unrealistic until conflicting national ambitions are resolved
rubrics_metrics.description: Disarmament (or preserving Europe in its existing condition) is inimical to progress and is unlikely while leading Powers possess unsatisfied ambitions; permanent settlement may require further wars to settle claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author views full disarmament as unattainable in the short run because unresolved national ambitions make guarantees ineffective; additional wars may define practicable settlements.

rubrics_metrics.name: A maturing nation should confine itself to practicable useful tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: The maturing nation is one capable of limiting itself to performing practicable and useful national work that advances civilization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: National development requires focusing on serviceable functions that accelerate 'the march of Christian civilization' (author's normative standard) rather than limitless expansion or abstract ideals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association and international engagement as condition of healthy nationality
rubrics_metrics.description: A nation that isolates itself loses discipline and experience; international association is necessary to develop national individuality and self-control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Isolation forfeits the 'discipline of experience' and wisdom from engagement; international relations are a necessary condition for healthy national development and for durable settlements.

rubrics_metrics.name: National identity grounded in historical association rather than abstract individual rights
rubrics_metrics.description: A nationalized democracy is not based on abstract individual rights but on accumulated historical association and community; societies lacking national tradition are less capable of nationality or democracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This view justifies tutelary colonial rule for societies deemed politically immature and frames democracy as embedded in national history rather than atomized individualism.
